subject: Geography
description: Cropping seasons, leading producer states, MSP, Green Revolution, recent farm laws

questions.stem: India's THREE main cropping seasons are:

options.option_text: Summer, winter, monsoon
Kharif, Rabi, Zaid
Tropical, temperate, boreal
Spring, autumn, winter

questions.explanation: KHARIF — sown June-July (with monsoon), harvested Oct-Nov. Crops: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, soybean, cotton, groundnut. RABI — sown Oct-Nov (winter), harvested March-April. Crops: wheat, barley, mustard, gram, peas, oats. ZAID — short summer season (March-June). Crops: watermelon, cucumber, fodder. Names from Urdu/Arabic — Kharif = autumn harvest, Rabi = spring harvest. India's agricultural calendar still revolves around these three.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India's largest producer state of WHEAT is:

options.option_text: Punjab
Uttar Pradesh
Madhya Pradesh
Haryana

questions.explanation: UP — largest wheat producer (~33-34 MT, ~30% share). Punjab — 2nd largest by output but #1 in YIELD per hectare. MP — 3rd. Together UP+Punjab+Haryana+MP make ~75% of national wheat production (most rabi). Largest RICE producer — West Bengal (or UP, varies year on year). Largest cotton producer — Maharashtra. Largest sugarcane producer — UP. Largest tea producer — Assam. Largest coffee producer — Karnataka.

questions.stem: MSP (Minimum Support Price) is announced by the Centre on the recommendation of:

options.option_text: Niti Aayog
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
RBI
Finance Commission

questions.explanation: CACP — formed 1965 (then Agricultural Prices Commission, renamed 1985). Statutory body under MoA. Recommends MSPs for 23 crops — 7 cereals (paddy, wheat, maize, ragi, jowar, bajra, barley), 5 pulses, 7 oilseeds, 4 commercial crops (sugarcane FRP, cotton, jute, copra). MSP intended to provide assured income (M.S. Swaminathan formula MSP = C2 + 50% margin — ie cost + 50%). Paddy + wheat have most active procurement (FCI). M.S. Swaminathan is called 'Father of Green Revolution in India' (received Bharat Ratna posthumously, 2024).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 'Green Revolution' in India during the late 1960s primarily focused on:

options.option_text: Tropical fruits
High-Yielding Variety (HYV) wheat and rice — particularly in Punjab, Haryana, western UP
Cash crops only
Tea and coffee

questions.explanation: Green Revolution — late 1960s, led by M.S. Swaminathan (Indian) + Norman Borlaug (American, Nobel Peace 1970). Imported HYV wheat (Mexican dwarf varieties — Sonora 64, Lerma Rojo) + rice (IR-8 from Philippines). Combined with assured irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides, MSP, FCI procurement — transformed India from food-deficient (1965-66 famine fears) to self-sufficient by 1975. Focus on Punjab-Haryana-W.UP because of irrigation infrastructure. Side effects — soil exhaustion, water-table depletion, pesticide use, regional inequality.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India's 'White Revolution' (Operation Flood) — making India the largest milk producer globally — was launched by:

options.option_text: M.S. Swaminathan
Verghese Kurien (under National Dairy Development Board)
Norman Borlaug
C.D. Deshmukh

questions.explanation: Verghese Kurien — 'Father of White Revolution'. Operation Flood launched 1970 by NDDB, Anand, Gujarat (HQ of Amul). Created a national milk grid linking producers across India to consumers in cities; cooperative dairy model based on Amul (Anand Milk Union Limited). India became #1 milk producer 1998; current ~22% of global milk output. Bharat Ratna posthumously to Kurien (in pipeline; not yet conferred). His birthday 26 November is National Milk Day. Operation Flood often called 'world's largest dairy development programme'.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India's 'Pink Revolution' refers to the rapid growth in:

options.option_text: Pulses production
Meat (especially poultry / pork) and processed-meat exports
Floriculture
Fruits like dragon fruit

questions.explanation: Multiple 'colour revolutions' in India. WHITE — milk; YELLOW — oilseeds; BLUE — fisheries / aquaculture; GREEN — food grains; PINK — meat (also onion / shrimp in some sources); GOLDEN — fruits / honey; SILVER — eggs / cotton; GREY — fertilisers; ROUND — potatoes; BROWN — cocoa / leather. India is now the largest exporter of buffalo meat. The 'Rainbow Revolution' is the umbrella term for pursuing all these together — agricultural diversification.

questions.stem: PM-KISAN scheme provides direct cash transfer to farmers of:

options.option_text: ₹6,000/year — paid in 3 installments of ₹2,000

questions.explanation: PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) — launched 24 February 2019. ₹6,000/year via DBT to all eligible landholding farmer families, in 3 four-monthly installments of ₹2,000. Earlier ceiling of 2 hectares removed in June 2019. Excluded: institutional landowners, current/former MPs/MLAs/ministers, professionals (doctors, CAs etc), pension >₹10,000/month. ~10 crore farmers receive benefits. ₹3+ lakh crore transferred since launch.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Black cotton soil — locally called 'Regur' — is ideal for growing cotton due to its high moisture-retention capacity. In which part of India is this soil type most extensively found?

options.option_text: Deccan Plateau covering Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat
Indo-Gangetic Plains stretching across UP, Bihar, and West Bengal
Northeastern hill region spanning Assam, Meghalaya, and Manipur
Eastern Coastal Plains along Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu coast

questions.explanation: Regur (black cotton soil) forms from weathered Deccan trap volcanic basalt and is most extensively found on the Deccan Plateau — particularly Maharashtra, MP, and Gujarat — which is why these states dominate Indian cotton production. The Indo-Gangetic Plains have alluvial soil (Khadar/Bhangar) that favours wheat and rice, not cotton, making it the most tempting wrong choice.

questions.stem: India is the world's largest producer of which natural textile fibre, with West Bengal alone contributing over 70% of the country's total output?

options.option_text: Cotton, primarily grown across Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Telangana
Jute, primarily grown across West Bengal, Bihar, and Assam delta
Silk, primarily grown across Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu
Hemp, primarily grown across Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh hills

questions.explanation: India is the world's largest producer of jute (the 'golden fibre'), contributing over 60% of global output. West Bengal, particularly the Hooghly basin with its moist alluvial soil, produces 70%+ of India's jute crop. Cotton is a major distractor but China and the USA compete at the top for cotton; for silk, China dominates global production with about 70% share.

questions.stem: Which quality-certification mark, governed by the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act 1937, is affixed to commodities like ghee, honey, wheat flour, and spices to certify their grade and purity?

options.option_text: FPO mark — certifies processed fruit and vegetable products only
FSSAI licence — certifies food safety compliance for manufacturers
Agmark — certifies quality and grading of agricultural commodities
BIS Hallmark — certifies standard quality of manufactured products

questions.explanation: Agmark (Agricultural Mark) is a certification administered by the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection (DMI) under the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937. It covers raw and processed farm produce — ghee, honey, atta, spices. FSSAI is a food-safety licence (post-2006), not a grading mark, and is the most tempting distractor; FPO is restricted to processed fruits and vegetables under a different Act entirely.

questions.stem: Chhattisgarh is called the 'Dhaan ka Katora' (Rice Bowl) of India. The state's fertile central paddy-growing plains are primarily drained by which river system?

options.option_text: Godavari river basin, covering Bastar and Jagdalpur plateau region
Son river basin, covering Surguja and Koriya highland districts
Mahanadi river basin, covering Raipur, Durg, and Bilaspur plains
Narmada river basin, covering Rajnandgaon and Kawardha districts

questions.explanation: The Chhattisgarh plain (the rice bowl) lies in the upper Mahanadi basin, drained by the Mahanadi and its tributaries — Sheonath, Hasdeo, Mand, and Ib rivers — which together irrigate Raipur, Durg, and Bilaspur. Godavari is a classic distractor because Andhra Pradesh is also called a 'rice bowl', but within Chhattisgarh the Godavari only drains the forested southern Bastar plateau, not the main paddy plains.

questions.stem: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), launched in February 2016, replaced which predecessor crop-insurance scheme that had been operational since 1999?

options.option_text: Comprehensive Crop Insurance Scheme (CCIS), introduced in 1985
Modified NAIS (MNAIS), piloted in 2010 on an actuarial-premium model
Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (WBCIS), started across states 2007
National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS), launched in 1999

questions.explanation: PMFBY replaced the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS, 1999) and its variant MNAIS (2010). NAIS had subsidised fixed premiums that led to massive government liabilities and slow claim settlement; PMFBY shifted to actuarial premiums with a capped government subsidy to speed payouts. CCIS (1985) was replaced by NAIS itself — a common confusion — while WBCIS uses weather-index triggers and continues as a separate complementary product.

questions.stem: Under the Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme launched in 2015, what is the correct combination of testing frequency and number of soil parameters reported on each card?

options.option_text: Once in 2 years, reporting on 8 soil nutrient and physical parameters
Once in 3 years, reporting on 12 soil nutrient and physical parameters
Once in 5 years, reporting on 15 soil health and chemical parameters
Once in 2 years, reporting on 10 soil nutrient and physical parameters

questions.explanation: SHC cards are issued every 3 years and test exactly 12 parameters: three primary macronutrients (N, P, K), one secondary nutrient (Sulphur), five micronutrients (Zinc, Iron, Copper, Manganese, Boron), and three physical/chemical indicators (pH, Electrical Conductivity, Organic Carbon). Candidates frequently guess 8 (forgetting micronutrients) or 10. Pesticide-residue testing is NOT part of the SHC protocol, so '15 with pesticide residues' is a planted trap for over-confident test-takers.

questions.stem: Under the e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) platform, once a farmer brings produce to a connected mandi, which entity is primarily responsible for conducting physical quality assaying before the online auction begins?

options.option_text: A designated FCI regional lab posted at each e-NAM connected mandi
NABARD-empanelled private testing laboratory located near the mandi
The APMC mandi itself, using its own appointed in-gate assayer staff
A SFAC-operated mobile van that conducts spot quality checks on arrival

questions.explanation: Under e-NAM, physical workflow remains within the APMC mandi: the mandi's own appointed assayers test the lot at the entry gate, generate a digital quality report, and upload it to the portal so remote buyers can bid online without physically inspecting the produce. FCI handles procurement and buffer-stock storage — not e-NAM assaying. NABARD and SFAC support agricultural finance and small-farmer agri-businesses respectively; neither manages mandi quality-testing under e-NAM guidelines.
